title: Kassapa's mountains
hook: the old ascetic loves the rocky hills, the rain, the elephants (Theragatha, Mahakassapa)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Talaputa the actor asked kada, when, and talked to his own mind. Your line was when will it be. Did you ask it kindly? Today, an old monk who isn't waiting for anything. He's already where he loves to be. Day eight hundred three.

Rocky slopes. Clear, cool water. Elephants trumpeting somewhere below. Rain sweeping over the ridge. It could be a postcard, but it's a run of pictures from the verses the Theragatha gives to Mahakassapa, the stern elder whom tradition remembers for keeping the strict practices: rag robes, plain food, the forest. Earlier this year we met him in that role. Today he does something softer. In his own song, he tells us what he loves.
screen: `ROCK, WATER, ELEPHANTS, RAIN.` → `THE STERN ELDER.` → `TODAY, WHAT HE LOVES.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain. After each picture of the hills, Kassapa says the same thing: those rocky hills delight me. He says it again, and again. The elder known for doing without is, in his own words, full of delight. Second, what's in the hills. Streams of clear, cool water. Slopes where elephants pass. The calls of birds. Rain on the rock. Room to sit alone. Nothing on that list is a luxury, and none of it belongs to him. Third, why the hills. His verses open by warning against going about surrounded by a crowd, where the mind gets pulled this way and that. The hills are the other side of that warning. They're where he can practice. So the delight isn't instead of the discipline. It grows right out of it. Fourth, the kind of joy it is. This isn't the joy of owning a view. Kassapa doesn't speak of owning anything up there. He comes, he sits, the rain falls, he goes down for alms and comes back. Some readers are surprised that a man of strict habits sings about beauty at all. The poem doesn't seem to feel any tension in it. A hard life can still have a place it loves, and say so without embarrassment. These hills delight me isn't a confession. It's simple news from the ridge.
screen: `THE REFRAIN: THOSE HILLS DELIGHT ME.` · `WATER, ELEPHANTS, RAIN, ROOM TO SIT.` · `AWAY FROM THE CROWD.` · `DELIGHT WITHOUT OWNING.` · then, large: `THESE HILLS DELIGHT ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a hill, or picture one. If there's a hill outside your window, find it. If not, bring one to mind: a slope you climbed as a kid, a ridge from a trip, the mound in a park. See its shape. The rock, the grass, the sky behind it. Let the breath slow down to the pace of something that doesn't move. When the mind wanders, come back to the hill. It hasn't gone anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Kassapa's mountains. The rocky hills the stern elder sang about: cool water, rain, elephants, room to sit alone, and his refrain that they delight him. Today's word.
Your line: these hills delight me. Today, name one place that delights you, and say so out loud, even if no one asks. Day eight hundred three.

howItsDone: Forest monasteries in the Theravada tradition are often set in hills and woods, and teachers read Mahakassapa's verses as a picture of how simple living and delight in nature go together.

his refrain is delight: those rocky hills delight me.
his verses warn against going about surrounded by a crowd
the hills are the other side of that warning: room to practice.
Kassapa's hills are empty of animals
elephants pass on the slopes, and birds call.

fork.setup: you're Mahakassapa, an old monk known for keeping the strict practices. someone asks if there's anything you love. what do you say?
options: the crowds who come to hear me.
fork.reveal: his own verses repeat it again and again: those rocky hills delight me. delight and discipline sit together in his song.

original.note: Pali: sela, rock, a rocky hill. The hills of Kassapa's refrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk enjoying a nice view.
what it means: Kassapa, known for strict practice, sings that the rocky hills delight him: delight growing out of discipline.
what a scholar hears: his verses repeat a refrain after each picture of the hills, te sela ramayanti mam, those rocks delight me.

notes: Thag 18.1 (vv. 1051–1090 as remembered). Confirm: the opening warning against going about with a crowd; the hill verses with the refrain 'te sela ramayanti mam'; clear cool water, elephants, birds (peacocks), rain. The voice says 'the calls of birds' to stay safe; confirm whether peacocks should be named.
'Earlier this year we met him in that role' refers to the dhutanga day (741, 'The strict practices'; 742 is the leper's offering). Confirm continuity.
Original: सेल (sela); confirm Devanagari, meaning and pronunciation.

Editor: cut the argument from silence that Kassapa 'doesn't build anything or claim a spot' (now 'doesn't speak of owning anything'), and replaced the myth item about building a dwelling with one the verses answer directly (elephants and birds).
Auditor (fresh review): script reads clean; corrected the day number in the continuity note.
